copy_units.text: Define the economic question before choosing an analysis task
Turn a broad social question into a bounded inquiry

Use computational, digital-trace and data-intensive approaches to investigate social processes, digital technology and society, while applying social theory, research design and ethical interpretation.

This area asks how social questions can be studied with digital records, computer-run analysis or simulations. A project still begins with a social question and checks whether its data and assumptions support the answer.
A short research plan naming the question, data or model, analysis steps, privacy checks, result and limits.

Analyse digital text or trace data only after defining the construct, platform/population scope, collection permissions and sampling limits; validate coding or model results against human-reviewed examples.

This work treats records such as posts or documents as evidence. The researcher defines whose records are included, how they were gathered, what categories or model are applied, and how the result will be checked against the original material.
A text-analysis report with the question, record sources, included material, category or model checks, errors and limits.
Build a reproducible workflow for a bounded social-science dataset: preserve provenance, clean and document variables, analyse a stated question, visualise results and report limits.
This work makes a data analysis repeatable: keep a record of where the data came from, how fields were cleaned or changed, which steps were run and how the result answers the question.
A rerunnable analysis file, a plain-language description of each data field, a results table or chart, and a note about decisions and limits.
Explore economic mechanisms with computational and simulation models

A computer model makes stated economic assumptions explicit and lets a learner compare what follows when one or more conditions change. A scenario is an exploration of those assumptions, not automatically a forecast of what will happen.
A scenario note showing the question, assumptions, changed conditions, compared results and what the model cannot predict.
Build and analyze economic evidence
This work turns an economic question into a usable set of measures, checks what each measure means and covers, and analyses the evidence without hiding missing or inconsistent records.
A checked data table and analysis note describing the sources, measures, comparison, findings and limits.
Analyze distribution, poverty, labour, and development outcomes

This work compares economic conditions across defined groups, places or time periods—for example, how income, work or access to services is distributed. Clear definitions matter because different measures can give different pictures of poverty or well-being.
A chart or table comparing a defined outcome across groups or places, with source dates, definitions and limits.
Interpret national accounts, labour, and public-finance statistics

This work interprets published economic statistics by checking what is counted, which people or institutions are covered, the time period and any revisions. It connects the measure to a policy question without treating a headline number as the whole story.
A short statistics brief that names the measure, coverage, period, trend, policy question and cautions about interpretation.
Evaluate economic or public-policy interventions

This work asks whether an economic or public-policy intervention was delivered as intended and what changed for the people or places it aimed to affect. When estimating an effect, the comparison must help show what might have happened without the intervention.
An evaluation plan or findings brief with the purpose, comparison, evidence, result, alternative explanations and limits.
Assess an economic or public-policy intervention by defining the outcome and comparison, checking available evidence and explaining the strength and limits of any estimated effect.

This work states the outcome and comparison before judging an intervention. It checks whether the available evidence can separate the intervention's contribution from other changes happening at the same time.
A concise evaluation brief showing the outcome, comparison, evidence chain, estimated or reasoned effect and limitations.
Use economic concepts and suitable data to describe a pattern or estimate a relationship; explain measurement, assumptions, uncertainty and what the result can and cannot say about policy.

This work uses economic ideas to describe a pattern or estimate how measured factors are related. The analyst defines each measure, checks the data and assumptions, and avoids treating an association as proof of cause.
A reproducible table or chart and an analysis note naming the population, measures, method, uncertainty and limits.
Examine people, place, migration, settlement, population change and spatial patterns in social and economic life.

This area examines how people and social or economic activity vary by place and change over time. A useful analysis states which places and people are covered and how the geographic scale affects the pattern.
A map or population profile with the data source, time period, geographic scale and interpretation limits.
Measure and explain population change using fertility, mortality and migration concepts, checking source coverage and assumptions before comparing estimates or projections.

This work explains population change by examining births, deaths and movement between places. Estimates and projections depend on definitions and assumptions, so they should not be presented as certain predictions.
A population profile or projection scenario stating the definitions, source dates, assumptions and uncertainty.
Describe how people, services or social conditions vary across places and scales by checking spatial data provenance, geographic units and map choices before interpreting a pattern.
This work maps or compares social conditions across places. The analyst checks how boundaries, map scale and data collection shape what appears to be a geographic pattern.
A map or spatial summary with the source, geographic units, scale, processing steps and cautions.
Use AI assistance cautiously when reviewing policy evidence

Computer systems that generate or summarize text may help sort a large set of policy documents, but a researcher must check each useful claim against its original source and record omissions or errors.
A source-linked evidence table showing the question, documents, checked summaries, exclusions, disagreements and remaining gaps.
Design a decision-linked citizen participation process

This work plans how people affected by a public decision can contribute before the decision is made. It states who is invited, what they can influence, how barriers to taking part are handled and how decision-makers will respond.
A participation plan naming the decision, groups to reach, questions, access arrangements, use of contributions and feedback to participants.
Analyse policy and political text as data when the question warrants it

This work examines speeches, policy documents or public submissions using defined computer-run steps to find patterns in wording or topics. Researchers check examples against the original text because language can be ironic, local or context-dependent.
A text-analysis brief stating the question, documents, categories or model, checked examples, patterns and interpretation limits.
Evaluate AI-enabled policies and public services

This work studies whether a public service or programme using artificial intelligence changes how the service is delivered or what happens to people using it. It checks benefits and harms across groups and does not substitute for a technical or legal audit.
An evaluation plan or report naming the service, intended change, comparison, groups affected, evidence, version or delivery context and limits.
Understand institutions, authority and policy processes

This work traces who has authority over a public issue, which bodies make or deliver decisions, who is affected and how a policy is put into practice. It describes the process without assuming that written rules match everyday practice.
An institution-and-policy map naming the issue, responsible bodies, affected groups, decision points and implementation questions.
Use community evidence and public records in local service oversight

This work brings community observations and public records into a structured review of a local service or project. A scorecard helps raise questions and agree on follow-up; a low score alone does not prove misconduct.
A source-linked scorecard recording the service, community criteria, observations, official response, evidence gaps and agreed follow-up.
Monitor and evaluate programmes or public interventions

Monitoring records what a programme did and who it reached; evaluation asks what the evidence says about its results, how they came about and for whom. The question and intended use guide which evidence is needed.
A monitoring or evaluation brief showing the purpose, activities, measures, evidence, findings and limits.

Turn a governance or public-policy question into a bounded evidence review: identify institutions and affected groups, compare evidence and options, then state a reasoned finding with uncertainty and trade-offs.
This work answers a defined public decision question by comparing credible information and feasible options. It separates what the sources show from assumptions, value choices and the recommendation.
A sourced policy brief with the decision question, affected groups, evidence, options, trade-offs, uncertainty and remaining evidence needs.
Design or interpret a political-opinion survey by defining the target population, question wording, sampling and mode, and explaining how nonresponse and measurement affect conclusions.

This work gathers comparable answers about political views or participation. The researcher defines who the survey is meant to describe, tests the wording and explains who did not respond and what that means for interpretation.
A survey plan or interpretation note covering the target group, wording, selection method, contact mode, response and limits.
Assess proposed or existing regulation against feasible alternatives
This work compares a proposed or existing rule with realistic alternatives, considering who bears costs, who may benefit, how the rule could be implemented and what evidence is uncertain.
A comparison table showing the policy problem, options, affected groups, likely costs and benefits, evidence and uncertainty.
Explore plausible futures and stress-test policy choices

This work explores several plausible future conditions and asks how a policy choice might perform under each one. The scenarios help test a strategy; they are not predictions that one future will occur.
A scenario set describing its assumptions, changes, implications for the policy choice and signals to monitor.
Diagnose behavioural barriers and co-design, test and refine an intervention

This work identifies a specific behaviour and the conditions that may shape it, then involves affected people in designing and testing a possible change. A small test can inform improvement but does not establish that the change will work everywhere.
A behaviour-change plan showing the behaviour, possible barriers, co-designed change, test, measures and safeguards.

Study a defined behaviour or social-psychological process by selecting suitable measures and an observational, survey, interview or experimental design; evaluate reliability, validity and ethical limits.

This work links a question about behaviour to a measure and a way to gather evidence, such as observation, a survey, an interview or an experiment. It checks whether the measure captures the intended idea and whether the study protects participants.
A short study plan describing the question, measure, participants, method, analysis, ethical safeguards and limits.
Analyse conflict dynamics and assess how an intervention interacts with them

This work examines the history, relationships and conditions involved in a conflict before judging a proposed response. It considers how the response could affect different groups and avoids treating one account as the whole explanation.
A conflict-context brief showing the groups, events, relationships, evidence, possible intervention effects and unanswered questions.
Examine how identity, group membership, social context or institutions relate to attitudes and participation, comparing appropriate evidence and alternative explanations.

This work asks how group membership, social conditions or institutions relate to attitudes or participation. It defines group categories carefully and compares other explanations before making claims about people.
An evidence brief naming the groups and measures, comparing accounts or results, and stating what cannot be generalized to individuals.
Use interviews, observation or documents to understand interaction

This work uses conversations, observation or documents to understand how people describe an experience or interact in a group. The researcher records context and checks interpretations against examples that do not fit.
A short analytic account linking selected excerpts or observations to an interpretation, context and counterexamples.
Analyse behavioural data when the question requires measurement
This work turns a defined behaviour into recorded counts, scores or categories and compares them in a way that fits the question. The measure and study design limit what any difference can show.
A results table or chart with measure definitions, comparison, uncertainty and a plain-language interpretation.
Study digitally mediated social patterns with computational methods

This work uses computer-run analysis of suitable digital records, text, connections or simulations to examine a social question. The researcher explains who or what the records represent and checks conclusions against context and assumptions.
A research note identifying the social question, records or model, analysis, validation checks, privacy steps and limits.
Gather situated evidence through fieldwork

Fieldwork means gathering evidence in the setting where people live, work or interact. The researcher records what was observed, the circumstances, their own role and how consent and safety were handled.
Contextual field notes and a short account that links observations or conversations to the question while protecting identities.
Interpret qualitative and mixed-method evidence

This work interprets words, observations or documents, and may combine them with numerical evidence. When methods are combined, the researcher explains how the findings connect and what remains different or unresolved.
An analysis memo showing themes or numerical results, how evidence was combined, points of agreement or disagreement and limits.
Analyze existing qualitative, documentary, and archival evidence
This work studies material that already exists, such as archives, reports, records or media. The researcher checks who created it, why, when, what is missing and whose perspective it records.
A source table and evidence-based account describing the records, their context, recurring patterns, gaps and limits.
Design and analyze social survey evidence

This work designs questions for a defined group, plans how people will be invited to answer, checks the questions before wider use and analyses the responses with the selection and missing answers in view.
A tested questionnaire, selection and contact plan, response summary and interpretation note with coverage and nonresponse limits.
Adapt and check social-behaviour measures across cultural or language groups

This work checks whether a measure makes sense in different languages or cultural settings before comparing scores. Translation alone may not preserve how people understand a question, so review and testing are needed.
An adaptation record describing the original measure, translation or wording changes, participant testing, comparison checks and unresolved limits.
Study social interaction through digital traces when ethically and methodologically appropriate

This work examines records of digital activity or links among people and organizations. It checks who uses the service, what the records omit, whether collection is allowed and how people could be identified.
A research plan or network/text summary naming the records, coverage, collection basis, analysis, privacy safeguards and limits.
Use language models as carefully checked assistants in qualitative analysis

A language model may help sort or summarize text, but the researcher checks its suggestions against the original words and context. The final interpretation remains the researcher's and errors or changes are recorded.
A comparison table with original excerpts, model suggestions, human decisions, correction reasons and privacy safeguards.
Study AI-mediated interaction and test social-agent simulations as experiments

This work examines how people interact with AI systems or how a computer simulation of social agents behaves under stated rules. Observed human responses and simulated outputs are different evidence and should be reported separately.
A study plan or report separating human-participant evidence from simulation assumptions, results, checks and limits.
Design, conduct and interpret qualitative, quantitative and mixed-method research to answer social questions and evaluate programmes or policies.

This area turns social questions into a plan for collecting and interpreting evidence. It may use words, observations, numbers or a combination, depending on the question; evaluation focuses on a programme or policy and its intended use.
A research or evaluation brief showing the question, evidence plan, analysis, findings, safeguards and limits.
Translate a social question into a feasible study design by defining purpose, population, evidence, sampling, method, ethics and the limits of the planned inference.

This work connects a social question with the people or records to study, how evidence will be gathered and what conclusion the plan could support. It includes privacy, consent and practical limits before data collection begins.
A study protocol describing the question, group or records, method, analysis, safeguards and limits on the conclusion.
Evaluate a programme by clarifying intended use and stakeholders, describing context and implementation, selecting credible evidence and methods, and reporting justified conclusions and limitations.

This work clarifies what a programme is meant to do, how it is delivered, who it reaches and what evidence can answer the evaluation questions. It separates evidence about delivery from evidence about results or effects.
An evaluation plan or report showing purpose, programme pathway, questions, evidence, findings, limitations and intended use.
Study social relationships, institutions, culture, inequality, communities and social change through theoretical and empirical inquiry.

This area studies how relationships, shared rules, institutions and cultural practices shape people's lives and change over time. It uses concepts and evidence to explain patterns without assuming every person in a group is the same.
Field notes, a source-based account or a comparison that explains a social pattern and states the evidence and limits.
Compare interview, observation or documentary accounts to describe a social pattern, explain how context shapes it and report differences or evidence that challenges the interpretation.

This work compares accounts from interviews, observation or documents to explain a pattern in context. It looks for differences and examples that challenge the first interpretation as well as examples that support it.
An evidence-linked account with excerpts or observations, context, alternative interpretations and limits.
Plan and conduct a qualitative interview to understand how people describe an experience, relationship or institution; record consent and context, then preserve a traceable account for analysis.

This work plans a guided conversation with open questions, obtains informed agreement to take part, records relevant context and analyses what was said without treating one person's account as everyone else's experience.
An interview guide, consent and data-handling notes, contextual notes and an interpretation linked to anonymized excerpts.
Estimate and evaluate an economic relationship or intervention

This work defines an economic outcome and the factors to compare, then checks whether the available data and study plan can support an estimate or evaluation. A relationship in the data is not automatically a cause.
A brief explaining the outcome, comparison, evidence, estimated relationship or effect, uncertainty and other possible explanations.
Build a forecast or nowcast with uncertainty

A forecast estimates a future value; a nowcast estimates a current value before all official information is available. Both depend on the data, time period and assumptions, so uncertainty and forecast errors should be shown.
A dated forecast or nowcast with the target measure, time horizon, data used, uncertainty range, checks and limitations.
Use AI/ML to construct or enrich an economic measure, then validate inference

Computer models may help create or improve a measure from several data sources, but the analyst must explain what the measure represents and test whether it works on new or held-back examples. Good prediction does not by itself establish a meaningful economic measure or causal result.
A documented measure-building report with inputs, target concept, data preparation, model checks, errors and limits on interpretation.
Interpret and compare qualitative material

This work compares accounts, observations or documents to identify patterns in meaning and experience. The researcher explains how examples were chosen and considers differences that do not fit the main theme.
A short interpretation supported by selected excerpts or observations, with context and counterexamples.
Explore social mechanisms with agent-based simulation

A computer simulation can represent people or organizations as separate decision-makers following stated rules, then show what group patterns those interactions could produce. The result explores the rules; it does not prove that real people will behave that way.
A model note showing the question, decision rules, assumptions, simulation results, checks and what should be compared with real evidence.
Computational and Digital Social Science

This area applies computer-run methods to social questions and studies how digital technology shapes social life. Learners may examine online records, text or relationships, or run simulations (computer models that explore what follows from stated rules). Programming is useful for tasks that need it, but it is not required for every learner or role.

This area applies computer-run methods to social questions and studies how digital technology shapes social life. Learners may examine online records, text or relationships, or run simulations (computer models that explore what follows from stated rules). Programming is useful for tasks that need it, but it is not required for every learner or role.
Use computer-based analysis to investigate social questions and examine how digital technology shapes social life.

Computational social science (using computer-run procedures to examine questions about people, groups and society) may study digital life itself or use digital traces (records created when people use online services, such as posts or transactions). A trace captures only the activity a service records; it is not a complete account of a person or group.

Researchers start with a social question and choose computer-run procedures that fit it. Some compare written material or measure relationships; others estimate patterns or simulate what could happen under stated rules.
An algorithm (a defined set of steps) sorts, counts or compares information.
Network analysis (representing people or organizations as points and relationships as links) measures patterns in those connections.
Text analysis (applying defined steps to written or spoken language) compares or classifies material in documents.
A statistical model (mathematical rules for estimating patterns or relationships) uses recorded measures to make an estimate.
A simulation (a computer-run exploration of stated rules) shows possible outcomes under those rules.
An agent-based model (a simulation that represents people or groups separately) applies rules to each and examines the group patterns that follow.
How do people in two selected online communities discuss the same public issue?
Which people or groups connect otherwise separate parts of an organization or community?
What patterns could form when people respond to one another under stated rules?
A study plan naming the question, records or model, analysis steps, privacy checks and limits.
A table or chart comparing patterns in selected records, or a simulated scenario that states the rules it used.
An explanation of what the result supports, who or what it may leave out, and what it cannot establish by itself.
Define the social question and the people, groups, place or period it concerns.
Check what the records contain and how they were created. Digital traces show activity on particular services; they do not automatically represent everyone affected by the question.

Choose a procedure that fits the question: compare documents, measure recorded connections, estimate a pattern or run a simulation. An agent-based model (a simulation of separately represented people or groups) applies stated rules to each.
Check the result against the question and available evidence. Explain missing information, choices built into the procedure and other limits before drawing a conclusion.

Online records may miss people who do not use a service or whose activity was not recorded. A model simplifies a process; a simulation shows what its stated rules produce, not what must happen in real life. A pattern alone does not show what caused it.

Public visibility does not remove the need to protect privacy, follow relevant service rules and ask for informed consent (permission given after a person understands what taking part involves) when it is required. A research ethics review (a formal check of how a study protects people) may also be required.
Economics and Applied Economic Analysis

Economics and Applied Economic Analysis study choices, production, markets, distribution, institutions and economic outcomes. Learners may use concepts, data and models to compare incentives or explain how a defined policy or economic change affects people and organisations. An economic estimate depends on its measures, assumptions and setting; it is not automatically a causal proof or a complete account of social life.

Economics and Applied Economic Analysis study choices, production, markets, distribution, institutions and economic outcomes. Learners may use concepts, data and models to compare incentives or explain how a defined policy or economic change affects people and organisations. An economic estimate depends on its measures, assumptions and setting; it is not automatically a causal proof or a complete account of social life.
Study choices about resources, markets and how economic costs and benefits are shared.

Economics (the study of choices about limited resources and how those choices shape production, exchange and living conditions) can be applied to a real-world question using evidence (information examined to support a conclusion). For example, researchers may examine how rising transport costs relate to household spending. Distribution (who receives benefits and who bears costs) is one question they can study.

Researchers define the question, outcome and comparison; find information such as prices, wages, business records or survey answers; and interpret the results using economic concepts. An incentive (a reward, cost or rule that can affect a choice) is one such concept. An economic model (a simplified account of how parts of an economy may interact) makes assumptions visible but leaves out some details of real life.
A resource-choice question examines how people, organizations or governments respond to prices, rules or incentives (rewards, costs or rules that can affect choices).
An economic model (a simplified account of how parts of an economy may interact) makes its assumptions clear so a learner can compare possible explanations.
A distribution comparison (checking who receives benefits and who bears costs) shows how an economic change may affect different groups.
How do changes in food prices relate to household spending in different income groups?
Who may gain or bear costs under a proposed tax change, and which assumptions affect that estimate?
How do jobs, wages or business activity differ across places or time periods?
A short economic analysis or policy or market note that states its question, evidence (information examined to support a conclusion), assumptions and limits.
A table or chart comparing a defined outcome across groups, places or time periods.
A clear explanation of what an estimate says and which choices or assumptions affect it.
State the decision or economic question, whose outcomes matter, and the place and period being studied.
Define each measure and find suitable information, such as prices, wages, output, taxes or survey responses.
Compare groups or periods, or use an economic model to examine a stated scenario; explain why that approach fits the question.
Describe the result in ordinary language, name other changes that could affect it, and state what further information would strengthen the conclusion.

A difference between groups, or a change after a policy, does not by itself show that one thing caused the other. Estimates depend on data definitions, the time and place, the comparison and the model assumptions. A result about one market or population may not apply to another.

Economic records can include personal or business information. Use data only for an appropriate purpose, protect private details and explain who or what the analysis leaves out. Economic estimates can inform decisions; they do not make the decision for the people or institutions responsible.
Human Geography and Population Studies

Human Geography and Population Studies examine how people and places are connected through settlement, migration, population change, access and spatial patterns. Learners may compare defined places or populations using maps, counts, rates, field evidence or other location-based information. A map or population pattern describes evidence within a chosen place and period; it does not by itself explain the cause or grant authority to approve a statutory plan.

Human Geography and Population Studies examine how people and places are connected through settlement, migration, population change, access and spatial patterns. Learners may compare defined places or populations using maps, counts, rates, field evidence or other location-based information. A map or population pattern describes evidence within a chosen place and period; it does not by itself explain the cause or grant authority to approve a statutory plan.
Study how people, movement, services and opportunities vary across places and over time.

Human geography examines how people and places relate: where people live, move and work, how settlements grow, and how access to services differs by location. Population (people in a defined place or group) studies examine how those people change through births, deaths and migration (movement between places). A spatial pattern (how people or events are arranged across locations) is one subject of study.

Researchers combine information such as census counts, surveys, maps, roads and service locations. They compare places at a geographic scale (the size of the area being compared), such as a neighbourhood, district or country. For example, a map can estimate what share of residents can reach a clinic within a chosen travel time, if the population, road and clinic information is suitable.
A population profile (a summary of a group's size and characteristics) describes how a defined population changes over a stated period.
A service-access map compares where people live with the location of a service and an agreed travel time; its estimate depends on the records and boundaries used.
A population projection (a calculated possible future based on stated assumptions) compares scenarios; it is not a guaranteed forecast.
Where are schools, clinics or transport services located compared with where people live?
How do population age, settlement or movement change across a defined place and period?
Which communities have longer journeys to a service, and what information would explain the difference?
A map or population profile that names its information source, dates, area size and interpretation limits.
A comparison of population change or service access across selected places.
A note that explains how place boundaries, missing records or travel assumptions affect the result.
Define the population, place, time period and question; use boundaries that fit the decision or social issue.
Check how population and location information was collected, how current it is and which groups or places may be missing.
Compare counts or rates (counts relative to a defined group or amount), or map services and travel routes. State which group or amount each rate uses.
Describe what the map or population profile shows and what additional evidence is needed to explain why the pattern occurs.

Maps depend on the boundaries and scale chosen; changing them can change the visible pattern. Place-level averages do not describe every person living there. Population projections (calculated possibilities based on stated assumptions) are not guaranteed forecasts, and a map alone does not show what caused a pattern.

Location and population information can reveal where people live or travel. Use the least identifying information needed, protect sensitive locations and check whether small or undercounted groups disappear inside area totals.
Politics, Governance and Public Policy

Politics, Governance and Public Policy study how public authority is organised, how decisions are made, how policies are implemented and how people participate in civic systems. The route can lead to evidence-based analysis of institutions, laws, programmes, international relations or governance outcomes. Learning this area supports analysis and advice; it does not give the learner legal authority, public office or power to make a decision on behalf of an institution.

Politics, Governance and Public Policy study how public authority is organised, how decisions are made, how policies are implemented and how people participate in civic systems. The route can lead to evidence-based analysis of institutions, laws, programmes, international relations or governance outcomes. Learning this area supports analysis and advice; it does not give the learner legal authority, public office or power to make a decision on behalf of an institution.
Study who makes public decisions, how they are carried out and how people can influence them.

This area studies political institutions (organizations and rules that organize public decisions), who holds public authority (the power to make or carry out decisions for a community), and how policies are chosen and delivered. Public policy (a government decision, rule or programme intended to address an issue) and governance (how public decisions are made, carried out and reviewed) are central subjects.

Researchers define the public issue, identify who can decide or act, and examine laws, budgets, meeting records, surveys or interviews. They compare policy options, including who each option may help or burden and what it may require to put into practice. Analysis can inform a decision, but the responsible public body makes the decision.
An institution-and-policy map (a guide to organizations, rules and decision points) shows who has responsibility for a public issue.
A policy-options comparison checks evidence, likely benefits and costs, who may gain or bear costs, and what administration is needed to put each option into practice.
A policy evaluation (a planned assessment using evidence) examines how a policy was delivered and what changed; it does not make the decision for government.
Which public body is responsible for a service, and how is that responsibility carried out?
Who can take part in a decision, and whose views or needs may be missing?
What benefits, costs and practical demands might follow from different responses to a public problem?
A policy brief that states the decision question, evidence, options, trade-offs and uncertainty.
A map of the organizations, rules, groups and decision points connected to an issue.
An evaluation (a planned assessment using evidence to judge how something is working) of how a policy or programme was delivered and what is known about its results.
Name the decision or public issue, the place and time, and the people likely to be affected.
Map who has responsibility, what rules apply and how people can take part.
Gather relevant records and accounts; compare options against the stated aim, evidence, likely costs and implementation needs.
Explain what the evidence supports, what depends on local rules or assumptions, and which decision-makers must consider the analysis.

Political systems, laws and responsibilities differ by country and level of government. A policy written on paper may be carried out differently in practice. Evidence can inform public choices, but it does not settle value disagreements or transfer decision-making authority to the researcher.

Political questions can affect safety, reputation or participation. Protect confidential sources, describe opposing views fairly and make clear which claims come from records, interviews or the researcher's interpretation.
Social Behaviour and Interaction

Study social behaviour and interaction as a social-science subject. This area does not include clinical assessment, counselling, psychotherapy, diagnosis, psychological treatment or professional psychology licensure; those belong under the separate Psychology and Counselling domain (D064).

Study how other people, group life and social settings relate to behaviour and interaction.

This area asks how people think, feel and act in relation to others and settings such as families, peer groups, workplaces or public spaces. Social influence (when other people or group expectations affect what someone thinks, feels or does) is one subject. In this D078 route, the focus is social research; diagnosing or treating mental-health conditions and qualifying to practise as a psychologist require separate training and professional approval.

Researchers define the behaviour and setting they want to understand, then choose how to record it. A measure (a defined way of recording an action, answer or experience) may be used in a survey, interview, observation or experiment. Researchers can compare what people report with what was observed. Each approach answers different questions and has limits.
A survey (a set of questions asked in a planned way) compares people's reported answers; wording and who responds affect what it can show.
Observation (watching and recording actions or events) shows what happens in a setting; the researcher's presence can affect what people do.
An experiment (a planned study that changes a condition and records what follows) can test a focused question, but its result applies only as broadly as its design and participants allow.
How do group expectations relate to what people say or do in a particular setting?
Do people's reported views differ from their choices in a specific situation?
How do relationships, roles or communication settings shape participation in a group?
A research summary that separates what was observed, how it was interpreted and what remains uncertain.
A table or account comparing defined responses or behaviours across settings.

Choose a suitable method and explain how participants, situations or responses will be selected and recorded.

Compare the evidence, consider other explanations and describe the conclusion only as broadly as the study allows.

What people report may differ from what they do, and behaviour can change across settings. A group pattern does not reveal every person's motive or diagnose an individual. A claim that a condition caused a behaviour needs a study design that can rule out other explanations.

Research may involve personal experiences or sensitive social settings. Explain participation clearly, obtain the required consent, protect identities and let participants know how their information will be used.
Social Research and Evaluation

Social Research and Evaluation focuses on designing, carrying out and interpreting studies that answer social questions or examine programmes and policies. It brings together suitable qualitative, quantitative or mixed approaches, evidence handling, interpretation and communication rather than requiring every method at once. The right design depends on the question and available evidence, and an evaluation cannot prove more than its coverage, comparison and assumptions allow.

Social research plans and carries out studies about people, groups and institutions. Evaluation (a planned assessment using evidence to understand how an organized programme or public policy was designed or delivered, whom it reached and what changed) is one part of this area.
Qualitative evidence (words, observations or accounts examined for meaning and context) can show how people experience a service or change.
Quantitative evidence (counts, measurements or scores) can show how much or how often something occurred.
Mixed methods (a planned study using both approaches) combines findings when they answer different parts of the question.
A theory of change (an explanation or diagram of how activities are expected to lead to results) makes a programme's assumptions clear enough to examine.

Evaluators agree what decisions the study should inform, define the intended result and choose evidence that can answer the question. A theory of change (an explanation or diagram of how programme activities are expected to lead to results, including the assumptions between steps) helps make that plan clear. Researchers may examine delivery, changes and costs; the exact design depends on the question and available comparison information.

Tracking activities or results is not the same as showing that a programme caused a change. A before-and-after difference may reflect other events. Stronger conclusions depend on the comparison, evidence, assumptions and setting; results from one programme do not automatically apply elsewhere.

Evaluation can affect services and the people who rely on them. Include affected groups where appropriate, protect personal information, explain how findings will be used and report gaps or harms as well as intended benefits.
Sociology and Social Anthropology

Sociology and Social Anthropology study how people live together: relationships, institutions, culture, communities, inequality and social change. This route can use theory, interviews, observation, documents or other evidence to explain patterns in social life. It is not a claim that one course or one study can describe every community, and it does not replace any professional licence or specialist training.

This route can use theory, interviews, observation, documents or other evidence to explain patterns in social life. It is not a claim that one course or one study can describe every community, and it does not replace any professional licence or specialist training.
Study relationships, shared ways of life, institutions and social change in their settings.

Sociology and social anthropology ask how people live together and how relationships, groups, institutions and culture shape everyday life. Culture (shared ways of living and making meaning, including practices, beliefs, language and expectations) is one subject. Sociology often examines patterns across groups and institutions; social anthropology often studies everyday practices and meanings in their setting. The fields overlap and do not use only one method.

Researchers begin with a focused question, then use evidence (information examined to help answer a question) suited to the people and setting. Fieldwork (research carried out in the place or community being studied) may involve careful observation, conversations, interviews and records. Researchers explain how they interpreted what they saw or heard and consider how their own position may affect the account.

In this area, R can help organize recorded behaviours or questionnaire answers, compare groups and show patterns in a repeatable way.

SPSS

SPSS Statistics is software for organizing numerical information and carrying out statistical procedures—defined ways to summarize or compare the numbers. Its procedures include comparing averages and checking patterns in counts across named groups.
In this area, it can help summarize questionnaire measures or compare groups when the question and the way the data were collected support that comparison.

For example, a researcher might compare average questionnaire scores for two groups or check whether response counts differ across categories. The choice of procedure depends on the question, the data and the procedure's assumptions.
A clear results table showing the relevant averages or counts and the selected procedure, plus a plain-language explanation of what the comparison can show.

An SPSS table does not show by itself whether the data, comparison or assumptions are suitable, and a group difference does not by itself show what caused it. Access and licensing can depend on a learner or institution.
Stata
Stata is software for organizing and analyzing numerical information and presenting results. It includes procedures for comparing groups and for studying records collected repeatedly over time.

When a study pairs interviews or other accounts with numerical measurements, Stata can help analyze the numerical part. It does not replace interviews or bring the different findings together by itself.
For example, you might compare a measured outcome across groups or follow the same households or schools across several years. The data structure and question determine which procedure is suitable.
A saved analysis script and a table or graph that reports the comparison or change, with a note about the data and limits.

Stata can carry out a selected analysis, but it cannot establish that the study design or interpretation is valid. It supports the numerical part of mixed-method work; researchers must explain how that result relates to interviews or other evidence. Access and licensing vary.

Computational and digital social-research methods

Computational social research uses computer-run procedures to investigate questions about society. These can include algorithms (precise steps for processing information), statistical models (mathematical descriptions used to estimate patterns) and simulations (computer-run models that apply stated rules to explore what could happen). The procedures may sort or measure information, estimate relationships, or examine what follows from stated interaction rules.

Network analysis maps people or organizations as points and their relationships as links. Text analysis uses computer-run rules to find patterns in documents; researchers check whether the results fit the question and the material being studied. Agent-based modelling simulates people or organizations following stated rules to explore how their interactions could create wider patterns. These are different approaches, and the choice depends on the question and evidence.

This approach can help when a question calls for comparing many survey answers, records, texts or relationships that would be difficult to examine one by one. It is one research approach among several; its usefulness depends on the question, the available information and the checks the researcher can make.

Digital traces are records created through people's interactions with digital services, such as posts, searches or transactions. For example, a researcher might compare how two online communities discuss an issue, map connections among local organizations, or simulate how stated interaction rules could spread an idea. The first two examine recorded activity; the last explores what the model's rules produce.

A short analysis plan naming the social question, information needed and its source, the computer-run procedure, checks for data quality and fit, privacy steps, and what the result could and could not support.
Digital records may leave out people who do not use a service or whose activity is not recorded; a pattern in the available records may not represent everyone.
A simulation shows what follows from its stated rules and assumptions; it does not prove that people behave that way in real life.
A relationship between two measured features does not by itself show that one caused the other.

JASP is menu-based software for statistical analysis. It offers t-tests (compare averages), ANOVA (compare averages across groups), regression (estimate how results relate to measured factors), and contingency tables (organize counts by category). Frequentist analyses interpret results against what repeated samples could produce under stated conditions; Bayesian analyses update stated starting probabilities using observed data. JASP calculates results; researchers choose a method that fits the question and data.

To ask whether first-year and final-year students use a campus service differently, you could organize their yes-or-no answers as counts and compare the pattern between the groups. If you compare satisfaction ratings instead, another analysis may fit. The question, answer format and study design guide the choice; a software result alone cannot explain why a difference occurred.

Network Analysis represents entities as points and their recorded connections as links, then examines patterns in those connections.
A family of methods for representing entities as nodes and their relationships as edges, then examining the resulting structure or patterns.

In this field, network analysis is relevant when relationships among people, organisations, places or digital entities are central to the question. Social network analysis is the social-science-focused branch when the nodes and ties represent social actors and relations.

Network patterns alone do not establish why ties formed or prove that network position caused an outcome.

Social network analysis
Social Network Analysis studies how relationships among people or organisations are patterned and how those patterns relate to a social question.
A way to study relationships between people, groups or other social actors by defining who or what counts as a node and which connections count as ties, then analysing the resulting network.

In this field it is useful only when relationships themselves are part of the research question. It is not the same as analysing social-media content, and a graph picture alone does not establish a social finding.

A network measure does not by itself explain a person's behaviour, establish causation or represent people outside the observed network.

Social Sciences & Behavioural Research

The social sciences are fields that study how people live together and how societies change. They examine relationships, groups and institutions (lasting arrangements such as families, schools and governments). Researchers ask questions and use evidence (information that helps answer a question), gathered or examined through methods (planned ways to gather or examine information). They describe patterns, compare explanations and show what the evidence supports.

Sociology examines relationships, groups and social institutions; economics examines choices about limited resources; political science examines public decisions and authority; social-behaviour research studies how other people and settings relate to behaviour. These viewpoints overlap and can be used together when a question calls for them.

Researchers ask questions, observe activity or examine documents, administrative records (information organizations collect while providing services) and digital traces (records from online activity, such as posts or transactions). They may count or measure information, interpret words or observations in context, or combine both approaches for one question. Researchers check who the records miss, protect private information and follow consent and participant-protection rules.
How do family, community, work and public institutions shape people's choices and opportunities?
How do access to resources or influence differ among groups, and how do people respond?
How do shared ways of life, organizations and societies change over time?
What evidence shows whether a public service or community programme reaches the people it was designed to support?
A research question and study plan that name whose information is needed, how it will be gathered and what the study cannot establish.
Organized survey answers, interview accounts, observations, documents or records, handled with appropriate care.
Tables, summaries or comparisons that show patterns and differences in the information collected.
A report explaining what the evidence supports, where it is uncertain and what a reader can reasonably conclude.
Start with a question about people, groups, institutions or social change.

Choose information that fits the question: a survey (a set of questions asked of people) gathers answers; an interview (a guided conversation) gathers accounts; observation (watching and recording what happens) records activity; document study examines existing texts or records.
Gather and handle information responsibly. Check what participants agreed to, protect private details and consider whose experience may be missing.
Compare the information with the question. Explain what it supports, what remains uncertain and what further evidence may be needed.

African and Nigerian societies
These courses examine African and Nigerian social structures, cultures, histories and regional settings.

You will study the histories, cultures, languages, institutions and social organisation of Nigerian and other African societies. Regional examples help you compare how societies differ and change. They are not presented as one story that describes every community.
Social work and practical change
These courses connect social-science knowledge with social work, community services, innovation and practical responses to social needs.

You will consider social causes of problems and the services and organisations that respond to them, then explore how social-science knowledge can support practical ideas and services. The curriculum’s examples are learning topics, not a guarantee of professional qualification.
Politics and organisations
These courses examine political life, collective action, formal organisations and how institutions work with society.

You will study how social conditions influence political activity, parties and movements, and how formal organisations are structured and operate. This connects institutions to the people and communities around them.
Ideas and foundations
Courses in this part introduce the concepts, history and theories used to make sense of the programme’s subject area.
You will learn how Sociology developed, explore key concepts and compare sociological theories. The programme uses these ideas to help explain social institutions, relationships and change.
People, groups and society
Courses in this part help you examine the people, groups, institutions, cultures or systems named in the programme record.

You will examine how people behave and relate to one another, and how families, groups, culture, language and social settings shape everyday life. The courses draw on Sociology, Anthropology and Psychology while keeping their different viewpoints distinct.
Research and evidence
Courses in this part show how the programme asks questions, gathers information, examines evidence and communicates findings.

You will move from forming a research question and planning a study to choosing suitable methods, collecting and analysing information, and explaining what the evidence can-and cannot-show. The curriculum includes quantitative approaches, which work with numbers, and qualitative approaches, which examine words, experiences and meaning.
Communication and academic writing
Shared university learning in clear English, reading, writing, reasoning and presenting ideas.

You will practise communicating clearly in speech and writing, understanding written information, and presenting ideas. These are shared university skills that support your Sociology studies. The course does not replace the discipline-specific research and reporting taught elsewhere in the programme.
Entrepreneurship and venture creation
Shared courses on identifying opportunities, developing ideas and understanding how ventures are planned.

You will explore how people identify an unmet need, develop an idea and plan a possible venture. These shared courses introduce entrepreneurship and venture creation. They do not promise that an idea will succeed or replace Sociology's study of social and economic conditions.
Nigerian peoples and culture
A shared course on Nigerian peoples, history, culture and social life.

You will study Nigerian peoples and cultures through historical and social examples. This shared course adds Nigerian context to your university learning. It is not a complete account of every community or a substitute for the Sociology programme's own African and Nigerian society courses.
Peace, conflict and security
A shared course introducing peace, conflict, security and ways people respond to conflict.

You will learn key ways people describe peace, conflict and security, and consider how conflict can arise and be addressed. This shared course introduces broad concepts. The Sociology courses examine particular social institutions, inequalities and settings in greater depth.
Philosophy and reasoning
A shared course on philosophical questions, logic and clear reasoning.

You will examine philosophical questions and practise logic-checking whether reasons support a conclusion. These are shared reasoning foundations, while sociological theory and evidence are developed in the Sociology courses.
Social change and development
These courses explore how societies change, what shapes development and how those changes affect people and institutions.

You will compare explanations of social change and development, then consider how economic, political and historical conditions affect families, institutions and communities. The curriculum includes African and Nigerian contexts as well as wider theories.
Inequality, gender and social problems
These courses examine inequality, gender relations, crime and other social problems, including their causes and effects.

You will examine how inequality and gender relations shape people’s opportunities, and how crime and other social problems affect communities. The courses compare explanations and responses rather than treating any single cause or solution as universal.
Technology and information
Courses in this part cover the digital applications and information practices recorded for the programme.

You will practise using a computer and common applications to create, organise and present information. The curriculum names these as general computing skills. It does not make a particular software brand a Sociology requirement.

Explore first, measure next
exploratory_sequential_mixed_methods

Use interviews or focus groups to discover local language, experiences or response options, then build a survey to examine how widely those patterns appear. The first phase informs the second. The two are not just separate studies placed together.
Qualitative inquiry -> refine concepts/questions -> pilot the survey -> collect and analyse survey data -> explain how the phases connect.
Choose this when the topic or likely answer range is not yet understood well enough to design useful survey items.
A small qualitative phase does not estimate prevalence; a later survey is only generalisable to the extent its sampling and measurement support that claim.

Measure a pattern, then explain it
explanatory_sequential_mixed_methods
A survey can show which patterns are common in the sampled group. Follow-up interviews can explore how participants understand or experience a surprising or important pattern.
Survey -> identify a result needing explanation -> select interview participants/questions -> analyse interviews -> integrate the explanation with the survey findings.
Choose this when the numerical result needs context or an explanation that the survey did not collect.
Interviews explain meanings and mechanisms; they do not independently prove why the survey pattern occurred or make the survey causal.

convergent_mixed_methods

Plan the shared question and separate strands -> collect/analyse each appropriately -> compare or integrate results -> explain agreement, disagreement and remaining uncertainty.
Choose this only when there is a planned integration question, not merely because both methods are available.
Different samples, measures or timing may explain disagreement; convergence does not automatically prove truth.

explanatory_qualitative_followup

case_study_multiple_sources

A case study is a bounded research design, not a single collection method. Interviews, documents and observation can reveal different sides of the same case. A survey or existing dataset can be added when the case question needs numerical evidence.
Define the case and question -> choose evidence sources that answer distinct parts -> collect and analyse each with its own method -> compare/integrate the sources -> report contradictions and gaps.
Use multiple sources when each contributes distinct evidence about the bounded case and there is a plan to interpret them together.
More sources do not guarantee better evidence; source access, quality, ethics and contradictions still need assessment.

qualitative_method_triangulation

Frame the shared question -> conduct ethically appropriate interviews and observations -> keep distinct records -> compare what each source can show and explain divergence.

Observation is selective and may change behaviour; it cannot reveal private motives without additional evidence.

For sparse categorical-count tables, choose the exact or justified resampling procedure when the large-sample chi-square approximation is unsuitable. The tests have different reference distributions and sampling assumptions.

For independent-binomial 2×2 data, Barnard's unconditional test is an exact alternative when conditioning on both margins is not required. Its an extra unknown value the test has to account for method, variance choice and sampling assumptions differ from Fisher's conditional exact test.

For independent-binomial 2×2 data, Boschloo's unconditional test is an exact alternative based on Fisher's p-value and may be more powerful. State the sampling assumptions and two-sided p-value convention.
For a two-group independent or paired contrast, a rank-based procedure may fit the outcome/design better. It targets a rank/distribution contrast and is not a drop-in mean test.

For independent groups, a rank-based overall alternative may fit when the inferential target is a distribution/location contrast rather than group means. Use a design-matched model when covariates or complex structure matter.

For complete matched blocks with one observation per condition, a rank-based repeated comparison can be an alternative to an appropriate repeated-measures ANOVA. It does not handle every unbalanced or incomplete design.
Probit and logit are alternative link functions for a binomial model of a binary outcome. Compare fit and predicted probabilities/marginal effects rather than raw coefficient scales.

For a prediction/classification goal, tree ensembles can compete with logistic regression as predictive models. Logistic regression remains a distinct inferential GLM and neither model establishes a causal effect.

For the same association question, use Spearman for ordinal/rank or monotonic association where Pearson's linear quantitative association is not the target. Related but distinct coefficients answer different questions.
For the same association question, Kendall is a rank-based alternative when concordance, ordinal measurement or tie handling better fits than Pearson's linear association.
Choose between rank coefficients by the result you set out to estimate, tie pattern, sample and inferential procedure; Kendall tau and Spearman rho are related but not numerically interchangeable.

For high-dimensional or prediction-focused work with collinearity, penalized regression can stabilize or select coefficients relative to OLS. Shrinkage changes estimation and interpretation, so this is a conditional specialist extension rather than a default replacement.

For continuous-outcome prediction, compare nonlinear tree ensembles with a linear baseline on kept-back test data data. The choice is goal- and validation-dependent and neither model is causal by itself.

Count regression provides an outcome-distribution-based inferential model; ML regressors may be compared for prediction but are not direct substitutes for its rate interpretation or inferential the result you set out to estimate.

For prediction/classification tasks, logistic regression can be a transparent statistical baseline beside more flexible supervised models. It is also an inferential generalized linear model. The goals and interpretations differ, so this is not a one-to-one equivalence.

When exploratory evidence suggests a measurement structure, CFA can test a theory-specified structure on suitable independent or kept-back test data evidence. Do not present this as an automatic step or reuse the same data without disclosing it.
Reliability estimates complement a specified measurement model. The coefficient and assumptions must match the scale structure, and reliability is not construct validity.
Reliability estimation complements dimensionality exploration but does not establish that the scale is unidimensional or valid.

IRT and CFA can address measurement structure and comparability through different model frameworks. Choose according to item response format, the result you set out to estimate, sample and assumptions rather than treating scores as equivalent.
ERGMs are a model-based extension for theory-driven inference about tie formation and network dependence. They require network-specific foundations and model diagnostics.
Spatial association analysis builds on defining units and a defensible spatial-weights structure. It describes clustering and dependence, not a causal mechanism.
Spatial lag/error models extend regression to specified spatial dependence and weighting structures. Diagnostics guide model assessment but do not mechanically choose a model.
Moran diagnostics and spatial regression may be used together to examine spatial dependence, but a significant statistic is not an automatic model-selection rule.
The ODD protocol supports transparent ABM specification and reproducibility; it documents a model but does not validate it.
This survey-specific application uses ML response models or ensembles for nonresponse adjustment. Survey design, weighting, variance and bias assessment remain essential.
LLM-based construct measurement is a newer text-as-data technique. Validate construct meaning, scoring stability and subgroup errors against credible references.
CA analyzes sequential interaction and participants’ displayed orientations; CDA examines discourse in relation to social practices and power. They can inform one study but are not interchangeable.
Process tracing structures within-case analysis of causal mechanisms using diagnostic evidence. Its explanatory logic differs from a population-level effect estimate.

Process tracing can examine how a proposed mechanism operates inside cases alongside a design estimating causal effects. Neither substitutes for the other's the result you set out to estimate or assumptions.

How you will use what you learn

Across your programme, you practise using ideas to ask focused questions, choosing suitable ways to investigate them, checking what the evidence can and cannot show, and explaining your conclusions clearly. The abilities below describe work your programme prepares you to practise; seeing them here does not mean you have already mastered them.
This learning is part of the official programme record. The outcomes below describe capabilities you are expected to develop, even when the record does not place them under a named theme.

You will practise communicating clearly in speech and writing, understanding written information, and presenting ideas. These abilities support your Sociology studies; they complement, rather than replace, the programme's research and reporting work.

You will study Nigerian peoples and cultures through historical and social examples. This theme adds Nigerian context to your university learning; it is not a complete account of every community or a substitute for the programme's African and Nigerian societies theme.

You will examine philosophical questions and practise logic—checking whether reasons support a conclusion. This builds general reasoning, while the programme's Sociology themes apply ideas and evidence to social life.

You will learn key ways people describe peace, conflict and security, and consider how conflict can arise and be addressed. This introduces broad concepts; the Sociology themes examine particular institutions, inequalities and settings in greater depth.

You will explore how people identify an unmet need, develop an idea and plan a possible venture. This introduces entrepreneurship and venture creation; it does not promise that an idea will succeed or replace the programme's study of social and economic conditions.

You will examine how people behave and relate to one another, and how families, groups, culture, language and social settings shape everyday life. The courses draw on Sociology, Anthropology and Psychology while keeping their different viewpoints distinct.
You will learn how Sociology developed, explore key concepts and compare sociological theories. The programme uses these ideas to help explain social institutions, relationships and change.

You will move from forming a research question and planning a study to choosing suitable methods, collecting and analysing information, and explaining what the evidence can—and cannot—show. The curriculum includes quantitative approaches, which work with numbers, and qualitative approaches, which examine words, experiences and meaning.

You will practise using a computer and common applications to create, organise and present information. The curriculum names these as general computing skills; it does not make a particular software brand a Sociology requirement.

You will connect social-science ideas with practical responses, including social-work services and innovation aimed at social or community needs. These courses introduce possible applications; they do not promise a particular job or business outcome.

You will study the histories, cultures, languages, institutions and social organisation of Nigerian and other African societies. Regional examples help you compare how societies differ and change; they are not presented as one story that describes every community.

You will compare explanations of social change and development, then consider how economic, political and historical conditions affect families, institutions and communities. The curriculum includes African and Nigerian contexts as well as wider theories.

You will examine how inequality and gender relations shape people’s opportunities, and how crime and other social problems affect communities. The courses compare explanations and responses rather than treating any single cause or solution as universal.

You will study how social conditions influence political activity, parties and movements, and how formal organisations are structured and operate. This connects institutions to the people and communities around them.

You will consider social causes of problems and the services and organisations that respond to them, then explore how social-science knowledge can support practical ideas and services. The curriculum’s examples are learning topics, not a guarantee of professional qualification.

Sociology is a social science: a field that studies people and how societies work and change. It examines how relationships, groups and institutions—lasting arrangements such as families, schools, workplaces and governments—shape everyday life and people's opportunities. Sociologists compare evidence across people and settings to describe patterns without assuming one person's experience speaks for everyone.

Sociological research begins with a question and a plan for gathering evidence (information that can help answer it). A survey collects comparable answers to planned questions; an interview is a guided conversation about people's experiences; observation means watching and recording activity; document research examines existing records in context.

To understand why students use or avoid a campus service, a researcher might compare interviews with observations or service records. Each source can answer a different part of the question. A pattern does not by itself show what caused it or apply to every setting, so researchers explain what their evidence supports and what remains uncertain.

top_level_journey_copy_units.text: The social sciences are fields that study how people live together and how societies change. They examine relationships, groups and institutions (lasting arrangements such as families, schools and governments). Researchers ask questions and use evidence (information that helps answer a question), gathered or examined through methods (planned ways to gather or examine information). They describe patterns, compare explanations and show what the evidence supports.

Your Sociology courses are a starting point for Social Sciences, not proof that you have mastered the field. Learn the three required foundations first. Then compare how research methods answer social questions. Choose a method or combined design to see linked domain learning, areas and roles; each item explains why it appears. Useful items are optional; conditional items apply only when stated. Course links record learning goals, not mastery.
Analysing social structures and societal dynamics; using core ideas about culture and socialisation; examining human behaviour.

Your Sociology curriculum introduces quantitative research and expects you to apply appropriate statistics. This route builds on that base with a more focused method and its choices; it does not assume you have already mastered every test or software tool.

Your Sociology curriculum introduces qualitative approaches and names examples such as interviews, focus groups, ethnographic work and case studies. The selected route gives a more specific explanation of the chosen approach and its use; it does not claim that every technique was taught in depth.

Your curriculum introduces choosing and justifying research methods. A named combined design goes further: it explains exactly how methods are ordered and integrated for a particular question. Selecting more than one method does not mean the curriculum or app treats every combination as the same design.
Your curriculum names the survey method. This route develops the selected survey work in more detail; it does not assume prior mastery of questionnaire design, sampling or analysis tools.
Your curriculum introduces in-depth interviews as a qualitative approach. This route explains how to plan and use interviews for a particular research question.
Your curriculum introduces focus-group discussion. This route explains how a facilitated group produces evidence, and what group discussion can and cannot tell you.

Your curriculum introduces ethnographic and observational approaches. This route adds the practical choices for recording and interpreting what happens in a setting; it does not assume that observation is suitable for every question.
Your curriculum introduces case study as a research approach. This route explains how to bound a case and choose evidence sources without treating a case as automatically representative.

occurrences.text: JASP is menu-based software for statistical analysis. It offers t-tests (compare averages), ANOVA (compare averages across groups), regression (estimate how results relate to measured factors), and contingency tables (organize counts by category). Frequentist analyses interpret results against what repeated samples could produce under stated conditions; Bayesian analyses update stated starting probabilities using observed data. JASP calculates results; researchers choose a method that fits the question and data.

occurrences.text: JASP is menu-based software for statistical analysis. JASP calculates results; researchers choose a method that fits the question and data.

occurrences.text: JASP is menu-based software for statistical analysis. It offers t-tests (compare averages), ANOVA (compare averages across groups), regression (estimate how results relate to measured factors), and contingency tables (organize counts by category). Frequentist analyses interpret results against what repeated samples could produce under stated conditions; Bayesian analyses update stated starting probabilities using observed data. JASP calculates results; researchers choose a method that fits the question and data.

occurrences.text: JASP is menu-based software for statistical analysis. It offers t-tests (compare averages), ANOVA (compare averages across groups), regression (estimate how results relate to measured factors), and contingency tables (organize counts by category). Frequentist analyses interpret results against what repeated samples could produce under stated conditions; Bayesian analyses update stated starting probabilities using observed data. JASP calculates results; researchers choose a method that fits the question and data.

occurrences.text: JASP is menu-based software for statistical analysis. It offers t-tests (compare averages), ANOVA (compare averages across groups), regression (estimate how results relate to measured factors), and contingency tables (organize counts by category). Frequentist analyses interpret results against what repeated samples could produce under stated conditions; Bayesian analyses update stated starting probabilities using observed data. JASP calculates results; researchers choose a method that fits the question and data.
