technical_term_coverage.glossary_definition: AAPOR (American Association for Public Opinion Research, a professional organization that publishes standards and guidance for survey and public-opinion research)

ABM (agent-based modelling: a computer-run study in which separately represented people or groups follow stated rules, allowing the researcher to explore what group patterns those interactions could produce)

administrative records (information organizations collect while carrying out services or official work, such as school enrolment or benefit records; the original purpose can affect what the records measure)
AfriSenti (a research dataset of social-media text in several African languages, created to study how computer models label expressed tone; language coverage and labels depend on the dataset)

agent-based model (a computer simulation in which represented people or groups follow stated rules and interact, letting researchers explore what group patterns those interactions could produce; the result is a modelled possibility, not a prediction of exactly how real people will act)
agent-based modeling (a computer-run approach that represents separate people, groups or organizations following stated rules, then explores what broader patterns their interactions could produce)
agent-based modelling (a computer-run approach that represents separate people, groups or organizations following stated rules, then explores what broader patterns their interactions could produce)
AI (artificial intelligence, computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing patterns, generating text or making recommendations)

AI RMF (the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, voluntary United States guidance for identifying, measuring and managing risks from artificial-intelligence systems; it is not Nigerian law)
algorithm (a defined set of steps or rules a computer follows to turn input into output)
algorithms (defined sets of steps or rules a computer follows to turn inputs into outputs)

ANOVA (analysis of variance: a test that compares averages across groups by comparing the distance between group averages with the spread of values within groups; it indicates whether at least one average differs, not which one)
API (application programming interface, a defined way for one software system to request information or actions from another)
ArcGIS (Esri software for storing, analysing and mapping information linked to places)
ARIMA (autoregressive integrated moving average: a method for describing or predicting values recorded over time using earlier values and earlier prediction errors; its assumptions must fit the data)
ARMA (autoregressive moving average: a method for describing values recorded over time using earlier values and earlier prediction errors; its assumptions must fit the data)
ATRS (Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard, a United Kingdom format for publishing information about certain public-sector algorithmic tools; it is not a Nigerian legal requirement)

AUC (area under a curve comparing how well a model ranks cases with an outcome above cases without it across different decision cutoffs; it summarizes ranking, not whether predicted chances are accurate or fair across groups)
autocorrelation (how strongly measurements relate to earlier measurements in the same time-ordered series; it can affect time-series analysis)
Bayesian (an approach that combines an initial estimate of what may be true with observed data to produce an updated estimate; the starting assumptions and evidence both matter)
Power BI (Microsoft software for turning information into interactive reports and dashboards; it does not choose a suitable research method or validate an interpretation)
bias (a systematic influence that can tilt what is measured, who is represented or how results are interpreted)
binary outcome (a result with only two possible categories, such as yes/no or used/not used)
CA (conversation analysis, a close study of recorded talk that examines turn-taking, responses and actions accomplished through conversation)
calibration (checking or adjusting a model so its outputs match observed results; in surveys, adjusting weights so totals match known group counts)

CAQDAS (computer-assisted qualitative data analysis software: tools that help researchers label passages in text, compare accounts and retrieve related material; the researcher interprets what it means)

case studies (detailed investigations of clearly defined examples, such as people, groups, organizations, events or programmes, using evidence that fits the question; one case does not automatically represent a wider group)

case study (a detailed investigation of a clearly defined example, such as a person, group, organization, event or programme, using evidence that fits the question; one case does not automatically represent a wider group)

CASEVO (Cognitive Agents and Social Evolution simulator, an early research tool for exploring social interactions among computer-simulated people; its output is not a validated stand-in for real behaviour)
causal (about whether one event, action or condition helped bring about another result; an observed relationship alone does not establish this)

causal inference (a way to assess whether a programme, event or condition helped bring about a change by comparing the observed result with plausible alternatives; the comparison and its assumptions matter)
CBN (Central Bank of Nigeria, the country's central bank, which publishes monetary and financial information)
CDA (critical discourse analysis: a way to examine how communication in specific settings reflects or challenges power, inequality and shared social assumptions)
CDC (the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: a public-health agency that also publishes guidance on assessing whether programmes work)
CDF (cumulative distribution function: a curve or rule that gives how likely values at or below a chosen point are)
centrality (a family of network measures describing a point's position or connections; each measure captures a different kind of position, not universal importance)
CFA (confirmatory factor analysis: a way to check whether answers to test or questionnaire items fit a proposed grouping meant to represent broader ideas, such as trust)
chi-square test (a test that compares observed counts with the counts expected under a stated assumption, such as no relationship between two groupings; it does not explain why a difference exists)
classical test theory (a measurement framework that treats a test score as a person's underlying score plus measurement error; observed scores are therefore not perfectly exact)
classification (assigning records to named categories using stated rules or a computer model; the categories and errors need checking)
classifier (a computer model or rule that assigns records to one of the named categories)
codebook (a guide listing labels for ideas in text or observations, with rules and examples for when to apply each label)
coding (labelling parts of information, such as interview passages, with categories so a researcher can organize and compare them)
coefficient (a number that summarizes a relationship in a model or calculation; its meaning depends on the method and scale, and it does not automatically show cause)
cognitive pretesting (trying questions with a small number of people and asking how they understood and answered them, to find wording that causes confusion before wider use)
computational (using defined computer-run steps or models to organize or analyse data, measure patterns or simulate scenarios; simply using a computer is not enough)

confidence interval (a range around a study's calculated result that shows uncertainty; with a 95% method, repeating the study under the same conditions would produce ranges containing the value of interest about 95% of the time, not a 95% chance for this one fixed range)
confounding (when another factor is related both to a possible cause and to an outcome, making their relationship hard to interpret)
construct (an idea researchers want to study, such as trust or belonging, that is not directly visible and must be represented through evidence or measures)
content analysis (a planned way to sort and examine communication, such as documents or posts, using defined categories to describe patterns in what is expressed)
conversation analysis (a close study of recorded talk that examines how people take turns, respond and accomplish actions through conversation)
correlation (a measure of how two quantities vary together; it does not by itself show that one causes the other)

counterfactual (a comparison idea about what would have happened to the same people or places without an intervention; both situations cannot be observed at once, so researchers use other evidence to compare them)
covariate (an additional measured feature included in an analysis because it may help account for differences in the result)
CPI (Consumer Price Index, a measure of how the prices of a defined basket of goods and services change over time)
critical discourse analysis (a way to study how language in context can reproduce or challenge power, inequality and social assumptions)
CRS (coordinate reference system, the rules that locate mapped data on the Earth's surface; mismatched systems can put layers in the wrong place)
CSV (comma-separated values, a plain-text file format for storing rows and columns of data)
DESA (the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, which works on economic, social and demographic issues)
DIF (differential item functioning: a check for whether people from different groups, but with similar levels of the quality being measured, answer a test or questionnaire item differently)
difference-in-differences (a comparison of how an outcome changes over time in one group versus a comparison group; it relies on the groups having followed similar trends without the intervention)
digital trace (a record created when someone uses a digital service, such as a post, search or transaction; it shows only what that service records, not the person's full life or views)
digital trace (a record created when someone uses a digital service, such as a post, search or transaction; it shows only what that service records, not the person's full life or views)
discourse analysis (the study of how language is used in context to create meaning, shape relationships or express power)
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid, inherited biological material that can help identify biological relationships; results require consent, privacy safeguards and careful interpretation)
document analysis (studying existing records by examining their content, who created them, when and why, and what they leave out)
edge (a line representing a defined relationship between two points in a network)
EFA (exploratory factor analysis: a way to find groups of test or questionnaire items whose answers vary together and may reflect broader ideas, such as trust)
empirical evidence (information gathered through observation, recorded counts, documents or direct experience, rather than a claim based only on opinion)
ESCO (European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations: a European reference system that groups job titles and connects them to skills and qualifications)
ethnography (research into a group's way of life, often through observation, participation, conversations or records gathered in context and over time)
EU (European Union, a political and economic union of European member countries)
evaluation (a planned assessment that uses evidence to judge how a programme, policy or action is working and what may need to change)

exact test (a calculation of how likely the observed counts, or more extreme counts, would be under a stated assumption, using the possible arrangements in the collected data rather than a large-sample shortcut)
experiment (a study in which researchers deliberately vary an intervention or condition and measure what happens; design and ethics determine which conclusions it can support)

factor analysis (a way to examine which test or questionnaire answers vary together and whether groups of answers may represent broader ideas, such as trust; it does not prove that an idea exists or is measured well)
FamilySearch (an online family-history service with historical records and a shared family tree; a suggested match should be checked against original records)
field notes (dated records of what a researcher observed, heard and decided while working in a study setting)
fieldwork (gathering evidence in the setting where people live, work or interact, while recording context and protecting participants)
focus group (a guided discussion where a researcher asks several participants shared questions and studies both their answers and how the discussion develops)
forecast (a calculated prediction about a future value based on information and conditions stated now; it can be wrong)
frequentist (an approach that compares a result with what repeated samples could produce if stated conditions held)
GDP (gross domestic product, the value of goods and services produced in an economy during a stated period; it does not measure every part of people's well-being)
generalized linear model (a statistical approach that relates measured information to an outcome such as a count or yes/no answer, where a straight-line model of the outcome would not fit)
geocoding (matching an address or place name to a location on a map; errors in names or coordinates can place records incorrectly)
GeoDa (software for exploring mapped data and patterns in how values are distributed across places)
geographic information system (GIS: software for storing, combining and mapping information linked to places)
GeoPandas (a Python library for organizing and analysing geographic data, such as boundaries and locations)
GFSM (Government Finance Statistics Manual, an International Monetary Fund framework for organizing statistics on government revenue, spending, financing, assets and liabilities)
GIS (geographic information system, software for storing, combining, analysing and mapping information linked to places)
GLM (generalized linear model: a family of mathematical methods for outcomes such as counts or yes-or-no results, using a form chosen to fit the kind of outcome)
GUI (graphical user interface, the buttons, menus and windows through which a person uses software)
historical research (a study that uses records, objects and accounts from the past to examine earlier events or change; who created each source, when and why affects what it can show)
homophily (the tendency for people with similar characteristics to be connected; an observed pattern does not show what caused the connection)
IBM (the company that develops SPSS software)
ICLS (the International Conference of Labour Statisticians, the International Labour Organization's forum for developing standards and guidance for labour statistics)
ID (identifier, a code used to distinguish one record or item from another)
ILO (International Labour Organization, the United Nations agency focused on work and labour standards)
IMF (International Monetary Fund, an international organization working on monetary cooperation and economic stability)

impact evaluation (an assessment of whether a programme plausibly caused a change, using a comparison to judge what may have happened without it; the comparison and the conditions behind it determine how strong the conclusion can be)
inference (a conclusion drawn from the evidence collected; it cannot safely extend beyond the people, places or conditions the evidence supports)
informed consent (a person's voluntary agreement to take part after receiving understandable information about the study, its risks and how their information will be used)

inter-coder reliability (a check of whether different researchers apply the same labels to the same passages or records consistently; agreement alone does not show that the labels capture meaningful ideas)
IPA (interpretative phenomenological analysis: a way to study how particular people make sense of important experiences, with the researcher interpreting their accounts)
IRT (item response theory: a family of methods that examines how a person's answers to test or questionnaire items relate to an ability or quality being measured)
IT (information technology: computers, software and networks used to handle information)
item fit (a check of whether answers to a particular question follow the pattern expected from the scoring method being used)
JAMB (the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board, Nigeria's national body responsible for tertiary admissions examinations and related processes)
JASP (statistical software with a graphical interface for running and reporting common analyses)
JBI (Joanna Briggs Institute, an evidence-synthesis and healthcare-research organization that publishes review methods and guidance)
KoboCollect (an Android application for filling and submitting forms built with KoboToolbox, including in some offline settings)
KoboToolbox (a platform for building forms and collecting survey or field information, including offline collection)

LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator: a way to build a prediction formula that can reduce some input weights to zero and keep a shorter set of useful inputs; selected inputs can change across studies and do not show what caused an outcome)
latent mean (the estimated group average for an idea that cannot be observed directly, such as trust, inferred from answers to several questions)
LimeSurvey (software for creating online questionnaires and collecting responses)

linear regression (a method that estimates how an outcome changes on average with one or more measured factors by fitting a straight-line relationship; it describes association unless the study design supports a cause-and-effect claim)
LISA (Local Indicators of Spatial Association, statistics that identify local clusters or outlying patterns in data linked to places; results depend on how places and neighbours are defined)
LLM (large language model, a computer system trained on large amounts of text to generate or transform language; its output can be wrong or invented)
logic model (a map linking a programme's resources and activities to its immediate products and intended changes, while making the steps and assumptions visible)
logistic regression (a method for estimating the chance of a yes-or-no result from measured factors; it shows relationships, not proof that a factor caused the result)
longitudinal (following people or other units, or measuring the same topic repeatedly, over time so researchers can examine change)

machine learning (computer methods that use examples from past data to find patterns and apply them to new information, such as sorting messages or estimating a value; performance depends on those examples and does not explain why a pattern occurred)
MAXQDA (software for organizing text, audio, video and images and labelling passages for later interpretation)
measurement (the process of representing an idea or feature with recorded observations, questions, counts or scores)
measurement error (the difference between the value recorded and the quality or event the researcher intended to measure)
measurement invariance (evidence that a test or questionnaire measures an idea in a sufficiently similar way across groups or times before their scores are compared)
mixed methods (a planned study that uses both numerical information and people's words or observations, then brings findings together to see how they agree, differ or explain one another)
ML (machine learning, computer methods that use examples to learn patterns and apply them to new cases; a prediction does not by itself explain why something happened)
model assumptions (conditions a model treats as true in order to calculate a result; if they do not fit the situation, the result may mislead)
model diagnostics (checks that help a researcher see whether a chosen calculation fits the data, leaves a systematic pattern unexplained or relies on conditions the data do not meet)
model fit (how closely a calculation's predicted pattern matches the pattern seen in data; a close match alone does not show that the calculation or its assumptions are correct)
Moran's I (a statistic that summarizes whether nearby places tend to have similar or different values under a stated map of which places count as neighbours)
multilevel (involving data grouped at more than one level, such as people within households or schools; the analysis must account for how those groups relate)
multiple comparisons (testing several groups or pairs; the more tests made, the greater the chance of finding an apparently unusual result by accident, so results need an appropriate plan)
natural language processing (computer methods for analysing or producing human language, such as sorting messages by topic; results need checking against the task and text)
NBS (Nigeria's National Bureau of Statistics, the national agency that produces and publishes official statistics)
NCRM (the National Centre for Research Methods, a United Kingdom research centre that develops and shares social-science methods training and resources)
NDPA (Nigeria Data Protection Act, the Nigerian law that sets rules for processing personal data)
NDPC (Nigeria Data Protection Commission, the authority responsible for overseeing data-protection compliance under Nigerian law)
negative binomial model (a way to analyze event counts when their spread is greater than a basic count model expects; the choice depends on the data and model checks)
NetLogo (a programming environment for building and exploring agent-based simulations)
network analysis (a way to represent people or organizations as points and their relationships as links, then measure patterns in those connections)
NHREC (Nigeria's National Health Research Ethics Committee, which oversees ethical review and monitoring for health research in Nigeria; its remit does not cover every social-science study)
NIST (the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology: an agency that develops technical guidance and standards for science and technology)
NLP (natural language processing: computer methods for analyzing or producing human language, such as sorting messages by topic; results need checking against the task and original text)
NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit, a Python library with tools for processing and analysing text)
node (a point representing a person, group or organization in a map of relationships)
nonparametric (using methods that do not require some specific distributional forms; these methods still have assumptions and can answer different questions)
nonresponse (when selected people do not take part or do not answer particular questions, which can affect what a survey result represents)
nonresponse bias (a problem that can arise when people who do not respond differ in relevant ways from those who do)
nowcast (a calculation about current conditions, made before all the usual information for that period is available)
NPC (Nigeria's National Population Commission: the agency that conducts national censuses and surveys and publishes the results)
null hypothesis (the starting assumption in a statistical test that the specified difference, relationship or effect is absent; the test asks whether the data would be unusual under that assumption)
OCR (optical character recognition, software that converts text in images or scanned pages into machine-readable characters; errors need checking)

ODD protocol (a three-part description—Overview, Design concepts, and Details—of a computer-run study where represented people or groups follow rules; it shows what the study includes and how it works)

ODD protocol (a three-part description—Overview, Design concepts, and Details—of a computer-run study where represented people or groups follow rules; it shows what the study includes and how it works)
odds ratio (a number comparing groups' chances of an outcome against their chances of no outcome; it shows how those chances differ, not that one factor caused the other)
ODK (Open Data Kit, a set of tools for collecting and managing information with mobile forms, including offline work)
OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, an international organization that publishes policy analysis and comparable data)
OLS (ordinary least squares: a method that fits a line or plane to data by choosing predicted values with the smallest total squared differences from the observed values)
OpenDroneMap (software for turning overlapping drone photographs into maps and three-dimensional models)
OpenLearn (the Open University's free online learning platform; course levels describe the study material, not a learner's qualification)
OpenRefine (software for inspecting, cleaning and transforming messy table data while recording changes)
OpenSesame (software for building and running behavioural experiments)
operationalization (deciding what observable information will represent an idea that cannot be seen directly, such as which questions or records will indicate trust or belonging)
ordinary least squares (a method that fits a line or plane to data by choosing predicted values with the smallest total squared differences from the observed values)

p-value (a number describing how unusual the study result, or a more unusual result, would be if there were truly no difference and the analysis conditions held; it is not the chance that a research idea is true)
parameter (a value that describes part of a model or process; it may be set by the researcher or estimated from data)

participant observation (a research method in which the researcher spends time in a setting, takes part where appropriate and records what people do; the researcher's role can affect what is observed)

Pearson correlation (a number describing how closely two numerical measures follow a straight-line pattern; it ranges from -1 to +1, and a relationship alone does not show that one measure caused the other)
PMI (the Project Management Institute, a professional organization that publishes project-management guidance and credentials)
population (the full group of people, places, events or records that a study aims to understand; it must be defined for the question)
PPU (Power BI Premium Per User, a paid Microsoft licence that provides additional features and has specific sharing requirements)
precision/recall (precision is the share of positive labels that are correct; recall is the share of actual positive cases the model finds)
prevalence (the share or number of a defined group with a condition or experience during a stated period)
PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses, a reporting guideline for describing how a review was planned and conducted)
probability (a number expressing how likely an event or value is, from 0 for impossible to 1 for certain under stated information)
probit model (a method for estimating the chance of a yes-or-no outcome using a curve based on the normal distribution; interpret results through predicted chances, not raw coefficients alone)
process evaluation (an assessment of how a programme was carried out, whom it reached, what activities took place and what helped or obstructed delivery)
process tracing (a method that checks evidence about the steps linking a condition to an outcome within one case; it can explain that case but does not calculate average change for many people)
psychometrics (the study of how tests and questionnaires represent qualities such as attitudes or abilities, and whether their scores are consistent and supported for the intended use)
PsychoPy (software for creating and running psychology experiments and related tasks)
PsyToolkit (a research and teaching platform for creating and running psychology experiments and surveys)
PySAL (Python Spatial Analysis Library, a Python library for studying how data patterns relate across places)
QGIS (free, open-source software for combining, analyzing and mapping information tied to places)
QualCoder (open-source software for organizing text, audio, video and image material and labelling passages for later interpretation)
qualitative (based on words, observations or accounts analysed to understand meaning, experience, context or process)
quantitative (based on numbers such as counts, measurements or scores, which can be compared or summarized using mathematics)

quasi-experimental (a study that compares groups or timing to judge whether a programme or policy may have led to a result when people were not assigned by chance; groups may already differ, so other factors could help explain the result)
randomized (assigned by chance, which can help make comparison groups similar on average; it does not remove every design problem, data-recording concern or ethical concern)
rank test (a test that compares the order positions of values rather than using their raw sizes; each test has its own design requirements)
README (a file of project instructions, setup steps or an overview that accompanies software)
precision/recall (precision is the share of positive labels that are correct; recall is the share of actual positive cases the model finds)
reflexive (carefully examining how a researcher's position and assumptions may shape the research)
reflexivity (examining how a researcher's position, assumptions and relationship with participants may shape the evidence and its interpretation)
regression (a family of statistical methods for estimating how an outcome is associated with one or more factors; by itself, it does not show that a factor caused the outcome)

regression discontinuity (a study design that compares cases just above and below a rule-based cutoff, such as a score that determines eligibility; it can show a local effect if nearby cases are comparable and the rule was not manipulated)
reliability (how consistently a measure or procedure gives similar results under comparable conditions; consistency alone does not show that it captures the intended idea)
representative (reflecting the features of a defined wider group that matter to the research question; this depends on who was selected, who took part and how missing responses were handled)
residual (the difference between an observed value and the value predicted by a model; patterns in these differences can reveal a poor fit)
RIA (regulatory impact assessment, a structured comparison of a proposed rule with alternatives and their likely effects)

AI RMF (the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, voluntary United States guidance for identifying, measuring and managing risks from artificial-intelligence systems; it is not Nigerian law)
ROI (return on investment, a comparison of a project's financial return with its cost; it does not capture every social or public value)
sample (the people, places, records or events selected for a study from a larger group)
sampling (choosing which people, places, records or events to study from a larger group; who can be selected and who takes part affects what the findings can say about the group)
SAS/STAT (the SAS software package for statistical analysis, including procedures for common research models and tests)
SAS/STAT (the SAS software package for statistical analysis, including procedures for common research models and tests)
scale construction (creating a set of questions or tasks to represent an idea that cannot be observed directly, then checking whether the items and resulting scores work as intended)
scoping review (a planned review that maps the kinds of studies, ideas and evidence available on a broad topic and identifies gaps; it does not necessarily judge which intervention works best)
semi-structured interview (a guided conversation with planned topics or questions that also allows relevant follow-up questions)
sentiment analysis (computer methods that label the tone expressed in text, such as positive or negative; wording, language and context can make the label wrong)
separation (in a logistic model, a condition where one or more measured features perfectly or nearly perfectly divide the outcome groups, making estimates unstable or impossible)
significance (the meaning or importance of something; in statistics, statistical significance has a narrower technical meaning)
simulation (a computer-run exploration of a process using stated rules or conditions, to see what outcomes those rules could produce)
SNA (social network analysis: the study of relationships among people, groups or organizations by mapping who or what is connected to whom or what)

social network analysis (a way to represent people or organizations and the relationships between them, then examine patterns such as who is connected to whom; the result depends on which relationships were recorded)
spatial analysis (the study of how locations, distance and areas relate to a pattern, using information tied to places)
spatial autocorrelation (how much nearby places have similar or different values under a chosen map of which places count as neighbours; it does not explain why the pattern occurs)

Spearman correlation (a measure that first puts values in order and checks whether higher ranks on one measure tend to go with higher or lower ranks on another; it can describe a steady rise or fall that is not a straight line)
SPSS (software for managing data and carrying out statistical analyses; the software does not choose a suitable method or make an interpretation valid by itself)
statistical model (a mathematical description that uses recorded numbers to summarize patterns or compare relationships; it simplifies reality, so its conditions and fit to the data need checking)
statistical test (a calculation that checks whether study results would be unusual under a stated assumption, such as there being no difference between groups)
semi-structured interview (a guided conversation with planned topics or questions that also allows relevant follow-up questions)
systematic review (a review that follows a planned search and selection process to find and assess studies about a focused question; it does not automatically combine their results statistically)
test data (examples kept separate from model-building and tuning, then used at the end to check how well the model works on cases it has not already learned from)
text analysis (a planned way to examine written or spoken language, by interpreting passages or using defined rules to identify patterns across many texts)
text mining (using computer steps to search or summarize patterns across many documents; the results need checking against the original language and context)
thematic analysis (a systematic way to identify and interpret recurring ideas across interviews, observations or other material; a theme is an interpreted pattern, not simply a frequently used word)
theory of change (a map or explanation connecting a programme's activities to intended results, showing the steps and assumptions that should be checked with evidence)
tie (a recorded relationship or connection between two people, groups or organizations in a network)
tokenization (splitting text into units, such as words or word parts, so a computer can process it; the chosen units affect later results)
training data (the examples a computer model uses to learn a pattern; if the examples do not reflect the people or cases it will meet later, its results may not transfer)
transcript (a written record of recorded speech or interaction, prepared using stated conventions; it may not capture every feature of the original)
transcription (turning recorded speech or interaction into a written record using stated conventions; choices about pauses, overlap and language affect what the record preserves)
triangulation (comparing findings from different sources, methods or researchers to see where they agree or differ; agreement alone does not prove a finding is true)
TV (television)
UK (United Kingdom: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland)
UKDS (UK Data Service, a United Kingdom service that provides access to social and economic research data and guidance)
UN (United Nations, an international organization of member countries)
UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, a United Nations agency working in education, science and culture)
UNSD (United Nations Statistics Division, the United Nations unit that develops and shares international statistical standards and data)
URI (uniform resource identifier, a text identifier for a resource; a URL is one kind of URI)
URL (web address used to locate a page or file online)
US (United States)
UTME (the Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination, the entrance examination administered by Nigeria's Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board)
validation (checking with suitable evidence whether a measure, model or procedure works as intended for the people, data and use in question)
validation data (examples kept separate from model training and used to compare or tune model choices before a final test)
validity (how well evidence supports the meaning and use a researcher gives to a measure or conclusion; a result can be consistent without measuring the intended idea)
variable (a named feature recorded in data that can take different values, such as a person's age, survey answer or income)
variance (a number describing how far values tend to spread around their average; larger variance means more spread)
weighting (giving some records more influence than others so an analysis reflects a stated design or known totals; weights do not automatically fix who was left out or how information was collected)
WHO (World Health Organization, the United Nations agency focused on international public health)

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: Use computational, digital-trace and data-intensive approaches to investigate social processes, digital technology and society, while applying social theory, research design and ethical interpretation.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: Use computational (using defined computer-run steps or models to organize or analyse data, measure patterns or simulate scenarios; simply using a computer is not enough), digital-trace and data-intensive (using large, varied or frequently updated collections of information that need careful organization and checking) approaches to investigate social processes, digital technology and society, while applying social theory (an explanation of how or why a social pattern or process may occur, which evidence can support, refine or challenge), research design (the plan linking a research question to the information needed, how it will be gathered, how it will be analysed and what limits the conclusion) and ethical interpretation.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: Analyse digital text or trace data only after defining the construct, platform/population scope, collection permissions and sampling limits; validate coding or model results against human-reviewed examples.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: Analyse digital text or trace data (recorded information used to answer a question, such as survey responses, interview notes or counts) only after defining the construct (an idea researchers want to study, such as trust or belonging, that is not directly visible and must be represented through evidence or measures), platform/population (the full group of people, places, events or records that a study aims to understand; it must be defined for the question) scope, collection permissions and sampling (choosing which people, places, records or events to study from a larger group; who can be selected and who takes part affects what the findings can say about the group) limits; validate coding (labelling parts of information, such as interview passages, with categories so a researcher can organize and compare them) or model (a simplified description of how a process or system may work, used to examine patterns or explore what could happen under stated conditions) results against human-reviewed examples.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: Explore economic mechanisms with computational and simulation models
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: Explore economic mechanisms with computational (using defined computer-run steps or models to organize or analyse data, measure patterns or simulate scenarios; simply using a computer is not enough) and simulation (a computer-run exploration of a process using stated rules or conditions, to see what outcomes those rules could produce) models (simplified descriptions of how processes or systems may work, used to examine patterns or explore what could happen under stated conditions)

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: A computer model makes stated economic assumptions explicit and lets a learner compare what follows when one or more conditions change. A scenario is an exploration of those assumptions, not automatically a forecast of what will happen.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: A computer model (a simplified description of how a process or system may work, used to examine patterns or explore what could happen under stated conditions) makes stated economic assumptions explicit and lets a learner compare what follows when one or more conditions change. A scenario (a possible set of future or changed conditions used to explore what might follow; it is not a prediction that those conditions will occur) is an exploration of those assumptions, not automatically a forecast (a calculated prediction about a future value based on information and conditions stated now; it can be wrong) of what will happen.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: Design or interpret a political-opinion survey by defining the target population, question wording, sampling and mode, and explaining how nonresponse and measurement affect conclusions.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: Design or interpret a political-opinion survey (a planned way to collect comparable answers from people, usually with a set of questions; wording, who is invited and who responds affect what the results can represent) by defining the target population (the full group of people, places, events or records that a study aims to understand; it must be defined for the question), question wording, sampling (choosing which people, places, records or events to study from a larger group; who can be selected and who takes part affects what the findings can say about the group) and mode, and explaining how nonresponse (when selected people do not take part or do not answer particular questions, which can affect what a survey result represents) and measurement (the process of representing an idea or feature with recorded observations, questions, counts or scores) affect conclusions.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: Study a defined behaviour or social-psychological process by selecting suitable measures and an observational, survey, interview or experimental design; evaluate reliability, validity and ethical limits.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: Study a defined behaviour or social-psychological process by selecting suitable measures and an observational, survey (a planned way to collect comparable answers from people, usually with a set of questions; wording, who is invited and who responds affect what the results can represent), interview or experimental (using a study in which researchers deliberately assign or change a condition and measure what happens; the assignment and safeguards determine what conclusions are supported) design; evaluate reliability (how consistently a measure or procedure gives similar results under comparable conditions; consistency alone does not show that it captures the intended idea), validity (how well evidence supports the meaning and use a researcher gives to a measure or conclusion; a result can be consistent without measuring the intended idea) and ethical limits.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: A research note identifying the social question, records or model, analysis, validation checks, privacy steps and limits.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: A research (a planned process of asking a question, gathering information and checking what it can show) note identifying the social question, records or model (a simplified description of how a process or system may work, used to examine patterns or explore what could happen under stated conditions), analysis, validation (checking with suitable evidence whether a measure, model or procedure works as intended for the people, data and use in question) checks, privacy (a person's ability to control access to information about them and how it is used or shared) steps and limits.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: This work examines how people interact with AI systems or how a computer simulation of social agents behaves under stated rules. Observed human responses and simulated outputs are different evidence and should be reported separately.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: This work examines how people interact with AI (artificial intelligence, computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing patterns, generating text or making recommendations) systems or how a computer simulation (a computer-run exploration of a process using stated rules or conditions, to see what outcomes those rules could produce) of social agents behaves under stated rules. Observed human responses and simulated outputs are different evidence (information examined to help answer a question or support a conclusion) and should be reported separately.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: Design, conduct and interpret qualitative, quantitative and mixed-method research to answer social questions and evaluate programmes or policies.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: Design, conduct and interpret qualitative (based on words, observations or accounts analysed to understand meaning, experience, context or process), quantitative (based on numbers such as counts, measurements or scores, which can be compared or summarized using mathematics) and mixed-method (a planned way to gather or examine information to answer a question) research (a planned process of asking a question, gathering information and checking what it can show) to answer social questions and evaluate programmes or policies.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: This area turns social questions into a plan for collecting and interpreting evidence. It may use words, observations, numbers or a combination, depending on the question; evaluation focuses on a programme or policy and its intended use.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: This area turns social questions into a plan for collecting and interpreting evidence (information examined to help answer a question or support a conclusion). It may use words, observations (actions or events watched and recorded in a planned way; setting, consent and the observer's presence can affect what is seen), numbers or a combination, depending on the question; evaluation (a planned assessment that uses evidence to judge how a programme, policy or action is working and what may need to change) focuses on a programme or policy and its intended use.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: Translate a social question into a feasible study design by defining purpose, population, evidence, sampling, method, ethics and the limits of the planned inference.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: Translate a social question into a feasible study design by defining purpose, population (the full group of people, places, events or records that a study aims to understand; it must be defined for the question), evidence (information examined to help answer a question or support a conclusion), sampling (choosing which people, places, records or events to study from a larger group; who can be selected and who takes part affects what the findings can say about the group), method (a planned way to gather or examine information to answer a question), ethics and the limits of the planned inference (a conclusion drawn from the evidence collected; it cannot safely extend beyond the people, places or conditions the evidence supports).

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: This work defines an economic outcome and the factors to compare, then checks whether the available data and study plan can support an estimate or evaluation. A relationship in the data is not automatically a cause.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: This work defines an economic outcome (a change or result that a programme, policy or process aims to influence; evidence is needed to determine whether it occurred) and the factors to compare, then checks whether the available data (recorded information used to answer a question, such as survey responses, interview notes or counts) and study plan can support an estimate or evaluation (a planned assessment that uses evidence to judge how a programme, policy or action is working and what may need to change). A relationship in the data is not automatically a cause.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: A forecast estimates a future value; a nowcast estimates a current value before all official information is available. Both depend on the data, time period and assumptions, so uncertainty and forecast errors should be shown.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: A forecast (a calculated prediction about a future value based on information and conditions stated now; it can be wrong) estimates a future value; a nowcast (a calculation about current conditions, made before all the usual information for that period is available) estimates a current value before all official information is available. Both depend on the data (recorded information used to answer a question, such as survey responses, interview notes or counts), time period and assumptions, so uncertainty and forecast errors should be shown.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: Use AI/ML to construct or enrich an economic measure, then validate inference
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: Use AI (artificial intelligence, computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing patterns, generating text or making recommendations)/ML (machine learning, computer methods that use examples to learn patterns and apply them to new cases; a prediction does not by itself explain why something happened) to construct (an idea researchers want to study, such as trust or belonging, that is not directly visible and must be represented through evidence or measures) or enrich an economic measure, then validate inference (a conclusion drawn from the evidence collected; it cannot safely extend beyond the people, places or conditions the evidence supports)

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: Computer models may help create or improve a measure from several data sources, but the analyst must explain what the measure represents and test whether it works on new or held-back examples. Good prediction does not by itself establish a meaningful economic measure or causal result.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: Computer models (simplified descriptions of how processes or systems may work, used to examine patterns or explore what could happen under stated conditions) may help create or improve a measure from several data (recorded information used to answer a question, such as survey responses, interview notes or counts) sources, but the analyst must explain what the measure represents and test whether it works on new or held-back examples. Good prediction does not by itself establish a meaningful economic measure or causal (about whether one event, action or condition helped bring about another result; an observed relationship alone does not establish this) result.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: A model note showing the question, decision rules, assumptions, simulation results, checks and what should be compared with real evidence.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: A model (a simplified description of how a process or system may work, used to examine patterns or explore what could happen under stated conditions) note showing the question, decision rules, assumptions, simulation (a computer-run exploration of a process using stated rules or conditions, to see what outcomes those rules could produce) results, checks and what should be compared with real evidence (information examined to help answer a question or support a conclusion).

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: Computational social science (using computer-run procedures to examine questions about people, groups and society) may study digital life itself or use digital traces (records created when people use online services, such as posts or transactions). A trace captures only the activity a service records; it is not a complete account of a person or group.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: Computational (using defined computer-run steps or models to organize or analyse data, measure patterns or simulate scenarios; simply using a computer is not enough) social science (using computer-run procedures to examine questions about people, groups and society) may study digital life itself or use digital traces (records created when people use online services, such as posts or transactions). A trace captures only the activity a service records; it is not a complete account of a person or group.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: Online records may miss people who do not use a service or whose activity was not recorded. A model simplifies a process; a simulation shows what its stated rules produce, not what must happen in real life. A pattern alone does not show what caused it.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: Online records may miss people who do not use a service or whose activity was not recorded. A model (a simplified description of how a process or system may work, used to examine patterns or explore what could happen under stated conditions) simplifies a process; a simulation (a computer-run exploration of a process using stated rules or conditions, to see what outcomes those rules could produce) shows what its stated rules produce, not what must happen in real life. A pattern alone does not show what caused it.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: Public visibility does not remove the need to protect privacy, follow relevant service rules and ask for informed consent (permission given after a person understands what taking part involves) when it is required. A research ethics review (a formal check of how a study protects people) may also be required.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: Public visibility does not remove the need to protect privacy (a person's ability to control access to information about them and how it is used or shared), follow relevant service rules and ask for informed consent (permission given after a person understands what taking part involves) when it is required. A research (a planned process of asking a question, gathering information and checking what it can show) ethics review (a formal check of how a study protects people) may also be required.

isolated_glossary_long_examples.raw_text: Economics and Applied Economic Analysis study choices, production, markets, distribution, institutions and economic outcomes. Learners may use concepts, data and models to compare incentives or explain how a defined policy or economic change affects people and organisations. An economic estimate depends on its measures, assumptions and setting; it is not automatically a causal proof or a complete account of social life.
isolated_glossary_long_examples.rendered_text: Economics and Applied Economic Analysis study choices, production, markets, distribution, institutions (established organizations or arrangements that shape social life, such as families, schools, courts or governments) and economic outcomes (a change or result that a programme, policy or process aims to influence; evidence is needed to determine whether it occurred). Learners may use concepts, data (recorded information used to answer a question, such as survey responses, interview notes or counts) and models (simplified descriptions of how processes or systems may work, used to examine patterns or explore what could happen under stated conditions) to compare incentives or explain how a defined policy or economic change affects people and organisations. An economic estimate depends on its measures, assumptions and setting; it is not automatically a causal (about whether one event, action or condition helped bring about another result; an observed relationship alone does not establish this) proof or a complete account of social life.
